position_in_era.historical_role: Same-era mutation: Jimmy Page's A–E–A riff at 158 bpm is the speed-and-momentum variant of the weight-first contract, simultaneous with Black Sabbath's self-titled album. Where Sabbath uses low-tempo dread, Zeppelin uses kinetic momentum — the riff propels rather than pins. The Norse-mythology lyric and Plant's banshee wail are the first documented pairing of riff-as-weapon with mythological narrative in rock.

narrative_slots.production_facts: Recorded June 1970 at Headley Grange, Hampshire, using the Rolling Stones Mobile Studio. Page's riff is in A, played at a gallop tempo with a shuffle rhythm feel. John Paul Jones's bass doubles the guitar riff in the verse; Bonham's drums are a force-of-nature addition. Produced by Jimmy Page.
narrative_slots.member_dynamics: Page (riff, arrangement) and Plant (vocal, lyric) are the compositional pair. Bonham's entrance after the intro riff is a documented shock-effect — his drums make the riff feel heavier on second hearing. Jones's bass doubles the riff, a Sabbath-style unison that gives the attack more mass.
narrative_slots.instrumentation_details: Page: Gibson EDS-1275 double-neck (live); studio: Les Paul through a Marshall stack; Jones: bass doubling the guitar riff; Bonham: Ludwig drums (the explosive entry is a single crash then lock-in); Plant: vocal. The riff is in A major/mixolydian, not minor — a major-key riff delivering menace through speed rather than harmonic darkness.
narrative_slots.cultural_venue: Released as a US single November 1970 (Zeppelin famously refused to release UK singles). Reached #16 US. The song was written after a Iceland concert — Plant's lyric is a report from the road, turned into mythology. The song's two-minute duration makes it the punk-brevity variant of the riff-first principle.
narrative_slots.release_circumstances: Led Zeppelin III released October 1970 — same year as Black Sabbath's debut. The simultaneous emergence of Sabbath's slow-dread and Zeppelin's kinetic-momentum variants of the riff-first contract established the two poles of hard rock for the next decade.
